title: "6. After Acceptance"
subtitle: "Lock your version permanently with two clicks"
filters:
  - reading-time.lua
---

Your paper has been accepted. Now it is time to permanently lock your code and data, publish your Zenodo record, and update your data availability statement.

This is the payoff for all the setup you did on Day 1.

## The acceptance checklist

### Step 1: Make all final changes

Incorporate all final reviewer and editor revisions:

- Update `analysis.qmd` if any analysis changed
- Update `index.qmd` for all text changes
- Re-render `analysis.qmd` to update figures
- Re-render `index.qmd` to generate the final manuscript PDF
- Update your renv snapshot if you installed any new packages:

```r
renv::snapshot()
```

### Step 2: Final commit and push

In Positron Source Control:

- Stage all changed files
- Write a clear final commit message:

```
"final version — accepted by Aquatic Conservation July 2026"
```

- Commit and Sync to GitHub

### Step 3: Create a GitHub release

This is the trigger that tells Zenodo to archive your code.

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 1
:::
Go to your GitHub repository in your browser
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 2
:::
Click **Releases** (right sidebar) → **Create a new release**
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 3
:::
Set the tag to `v1.0` and the title to something like:
`"Final accepted version — Aquatic Conservation"`
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 4
:::
Click **Publish release**
:::

Zenodo automatically detects this release, archives a permanent snapshot of your entire repository at that exact point, and assigns your reserved DOI to it.

### Step 4: Publish your Zenodo record

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 1
:::
Go to [zenodo.org](https://zenodo.org) and find your draft record
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 2
:::
Check and update the metadata if needed — title, authors, description
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 3
:::
Add the published paper DOI in the "Related identifiers" field once you have it
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 4
:::
Set license: **CC BY 4.0** for data, **MIT** for code
:::

::: {.step-box}
::: {.step-label}
Step 5
:::
Click **Publish** — the record is now permanently locked and publicly available
:::

::: {.callout-important}
### Once published, a Zenodo record cannot be deleted
This is intentional — permanent archiving means permanent. You can upload a new version (which gets a new DOI), but the original record stays. Make sure your metadata is correct before clicking Publish.
:::

### Step 5: Update your data availability statement

Replace the "upon acceptance" note in your final manuscript:

**Before:**
```
Data and code are available on Zenodo at 
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234567 
(will be made publicly available upon acceptance).
```

**After:**
```
Data and code supporting this study are available on 
Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234567 
and on GitHub at 
https://github.com/yourusername/koura-habitat-mesocosm.
```

## The complete timeline

| When | Action | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Create project, init Git, push to GitHub | Positron |
| Day 1 | Connect GitHub to Zenodo | Zenodo |
| Day 1 | Set up renv | Positron terminal |
| Throughout | Commit and sync regularly | Positron |
| Submission | Reserve Zenodo DOI (draft) | Zenodo |
| Submission | Add DOI + GitHub link to manuscript | index.qmd |
| During review | Continue committing revisions | Positron |
| Acceptance | Final commit and push | Positron |
| Acceptance | Create GitHub release v1.0 | GitHub website |
| Acceptance | Publish Zenodo record | Zenodo website |
| Acceptance | Update data availability statement | index.qmd |
| Published | Cite DOI in future work | Everywhere |

## What you have now

After following this workflow, you have:

- A complete version history of every decision made during the research
- A publicly accessible code repository that reviewers and readers can explore
- A permanent, citable archive with a DOI that will work forever
- A fully reproducible analysis — anyone can clone your repository, run `renv::restore()`, render `analysis.qmd`, and reproduce every figure and result
- A manuscript that was produced directly from the same code, eliminating copy-paste errors

::: {.callout-note}
### This guide itself follows this workflow
This guide was written in Quarto and version controlled on GitHub. A permanent Zenodo DOI will be added once it is archived. The source code is available at [github.com/OlivierRaven/Open_Research_Workflow](https://github.com/OlivierRaven/Open_Research_Workflow).
:::
